items.title: Peak age and epidemiology
items.contentHtml:
Peak age 2-6 years

  • Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (APGN) is the most common cause of acute glomerulonephritis in childhood, with peak incidence between 2 and 6 years.
  • It predominates in males (2:1) and is more common in developing countries or overcrowded conditions.
  • The main differential diagnosis in this range Age includes IgA nephropathy (more common in young adults and adolescents), but PGNAS is characterized by epidemic or sporadic presentation after streptococcal infection.
  • In children under 2 years of age it is rare, and if it occurs, consider other causes of hematuria, such as uropathies or Alport's disease.

items.title: Latency period
items.contentHtml:
Latency 1-3 weeks

  • The latency between infection and nephritis is 1 to 3 weeks; typically 1-2 weeks after pharyngitis and 3-6 weeks after impetigo (although the classic focus says 1-3 weeks, remember the difference by site).
  • This interval is key to differentiate from IgA nephropathy, where hematuria appears within 1-2 days from an upper respiratory infection (synchronous hematuria).
  • Long latency indicates that the injury is mediated by immune complexes, not by direct bacterial invasion.
  • Examination question: If hematuria occurs after 2 days, it is not GNAPE; think IgA nephropathy.

items.title: Plugin Profile
items.contentHtml:
Low C3 with normal C4

  • Classic finding: Low C3 with normal C4 (alternate pathway activated).
  • Total serum complement (CH50) is also decreased, but C3 is the most sensitive marker.
  • C3 usually normalizes in 6-8 weeks; if it persists for more than 8 weeks, consider other causes such as lupus nephritis or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
  • In the biopsy, immunofluorescence shows granular deposits of C3 and IgG (“chain of beads” pattern); If there is only C3, suspect dense deposit disease.

items.title: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
items.contentHtml:
ASO elevated after pharyngitis

  • The antistreptolysin O (ASO) is elevated in 80-85% of cases after pharyngitis, but only in 30-50% after impetigo (because cholesterol in the skin inhibits streptolysin O).
  • The maximum titer is reached at 3-6 weeksand it may take months to normalize; A single high titer does not confirm recent infection, serial elevation is required.
  • If the ASO is negative and there is suspicion, order other tests: anti-DNase B, anti-hyaluronidase, anti-streptokinase.
  • In the context of pharyngitis, the ASO is the first test; If the patient had impetigo, anti-DNase B is more sensitive.

items.title: Anti-DNase B
items.contentHtml:
Anti-DNase B after impetigo

  • The anti-DNase B is the marker of choice when skin infection (impetigo) is the antecedent, with sensitivity >90%.
  • It rises more slowly than the ASO (peak at 6-8 weeks) and remains elevated for longer, useful for late diagnosis.
  • Combine ASO and anti-DNase B increase the sensitivity to detect recent streptococcal infection up to 95%.
  • Do not use these antibodies to monitor the evolution of nephritis; They only confirm the etiology.

items.title: Hematuria
items.contentHtml:
Choleuric and dysmorphic hematuria

  • Hematuria is choluric (“cola” or “tea” colored urine) and dysmorphic (deformed red blood cells in sediment).
  • Macroscopic hematuria occurs in 30-50% of children; microscopic is almost universal.
  • Dysmorphic red cells, erythrocyte casts and proteinuria (typically subnephrotic, <3 g/day) are observed in the urinary sediment.
  • Macroscopic hematuria usually resolves in 1-2 weeks; microscopic can persist for 1-2 years.
  • The presence of erythrocyte casts confirms glomerular origin.

items.title: nephritic syndrome
items.contentHtml:
Acute hypertension and edema

  • The classic triad: arterial hypertension, edema and hematuria; Hypertension is due to volume expansion due to sodium and water retention, not hyperreninemia.
  • The edema is periorbital and of the lower limbs, often with signs of volume overload (jugular engorgement, tachypnea).
  • In severe cases there may be hypertensive encephalopathy (seizures, headache) or acute pulmonary edema.
  • Treatment of hypertension is with loop diuretics (furosemide 1-2 mg/kg/dose) and sodium restriction; if there is a hypertensive emergency, use vasodilators such as intravenous hydralazine.
  • Do not use angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors as first line in the acute phase, since hypertension is volume-dependent.

items.title: Oliguria and kidney function
items.contentHtml:
Oliguria with renal failure

  • Oliguria (diuresis <0.5 ml/kg/h) occurs in the acute phase and may be accompanied by acute renal failure with elevated creatinine.
  • Renal failure is generally mild and transient; the need for dialysis occurs in <2% of children.
  • Nitrogen retention (azotemia) is disproportionate to the drop in glomerular filtration, due to hypercatabolism.
  • Management: fluid restriction (only replacing insensible losses plus diuresis), diuretics, and electrolyte control (risk of hyperkalemia).
  • Kidney function normalizes in the majority in 2-4 weeks; If deterioration persists for more than 6-8 weeks, consider biopsy.

items.title: Biopsy indications
items.contentHtml:
Indication for renal biopsy

  • Biopsy is NOT routine in children with typical presentation and expected evolution.
  • Indications: persistent low C3 complement for more than 8 weeks, nephrotic syndrome (coexisting proteinuria >3.5 g/day), rapidly progressive renal failure, prolonged anuria (>1 week) or absence of recovery of renal function at 6-8 weeks.
  • Also if the presentation is atypical: age <2 years, without evidence of streptococcal infection, or family history of nephropathy.
  • In the biopsy, electron microscopy shows subepithelial deposits in the shape of a “hump” (humps).

items.title: Forecast
items.contentHtml:
Excellent prognosis in children

  • The prognosis is excellent in children: complete recovery in >95% of cases.
  • Microscopic hematuria may persist up to 1-2 years, but does not indicate a poor prognosis.
  • Poor prognostic factors: advanced age (adults), nephrotic syndrome, prolonged oliguric renal failure, and biopsy with extracapillary proliferation extensive (crescents).
  • In adults, up to 30-50% may have long-term hypertension or proteinuria, but in children progression to chronic kidney disease is rare (<1%).

items.title: Antibiotic treatment
items.contentHtml:
Does not require prophylactic antibiotics

  • Once glomerulonephritis is established, does not require prophylactic antibiotics; kidney damage is already mediated by immune complexes and not by live bacteria.
  • If there is active streptococcal infection (pharyngitis or impetigo) at the time of diagnosis, it is treated with antibiotics to eradicate the germ and prevent dissemination, but it does not modify renal evolution.
  • Treatment of choice: oral penicillin V (children: 50 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours by 10 days) or intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (600,000 U if weight <27 kg; 1,200,000 U if >27 kg).
  • In those allergic to penicillin, use erythromycin or clindamycin.
  • Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended cohabitants or for the patient, except in epidemic outbreaks.

items.title: Symptomatic management
items.contentHtml:
Symptomatic treatment and diuretics

  • The mainstay is symptomatic treatment: relative rest, sodium and fluid restriction, and blood pressure control.
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide 1-2 mg/kg/dose oral or intravenous) are indicated if there is significant edema, hypertension, or volume overload.
  • Hypertension mild can be managed alone with diuretics and sodium restriction; if it persists, add amlodipine (0.1-0.2 mg/kg/day) or nifedipine.
  • In hypertensive emergency, use intravenous hydralazine (0.1-0.2 mg/kg/dose) or intravenous labetalol.
  • Do not use corticosteroids or immunosuppressants; GNAPE is a self-limiting disease.
  • Indication for dialysis: severe hyperkalemia, refractory metabolic acidosis, acute lung edema or symptomatic uremia.
